scenes.name: Sugar Hill Records y Rapper’s Delight
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Sylvia Robinson, la «madre del hip hop», venía del R&B: Little Sylvia, el dúo Mickey & Sylvia («Love Is Strange», 1956), la producción del «It’s Gonna Work Out Fine» de Ike & Tina, el sello All Platinum con su marido Joe (con supuestos lazos mafiosos) y su propio éxito «Pillow Talk» (1973). Arruinada, vio a Lovebug Starski en Harlem World en 1979 y quiso grabar aquello; con Morris Levy fundaron Sugar Hill. Su hijo la llevó a una pizzería de Nueva Jersey donde Big Bank Hank, mánager de los Cold Crush, hizo una audición en su coche junto a Master Gee y Wonder Mike: la Sugarhill Gang. Sobre una recreación de «Good Times» de Chic grabaron quince minutos de rimas que una radio de St. Louis, WESL, se atrevió a poner: «Rapper’s Delight» inundó el mundo en otoño de 1979, dejó en anécdota el «King Tim III» de Fatback y demostró que el hip hop era negocio. En el Bronx sonaba a imitación higienizada: Hank rapeaba las rimas de Grandmaster Caz («I’m the C-A-S-AN, the O-V-A»), un estribillo de Hollywood y una frase de Rahiem; «hizo retroceder el hip hop cinco años» (Charlie Chase). Para Kool Moe Dee, sin Sugar Hill quizá no habría industria. La casa no pagaba bien a sus artistas, y su banda (Skip Alexander, Doug Wimbish, Duke Bootee) tocaba los temas. En Harlem, Bobby Robinson y su sello Enjoy ficharon a Flash, los Funky 4 + 1 y los Treacherous Three.

scenes.name: Sweet funk: el soul sexual
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras Let’s Get It On, «Me and Mrs. Jones» de Billy Paul y «Let’s Stay Together» de Al Green llegó una nueva hornada de cantantes sensuales. Barry White, con su orquesta de estudio sobre una sección rítmica de R&B, unió la elegancia occidental y la sensualidad negra: un lujo negro impensable diez años antes. Los Moments («Sexy Mama»), Main Ingredient, los Miracles («Do It Baby»), Leon Haywood («I Want’a Do Something Freaky to You», base de «Nothin’ but a G Thang» de Dr. Dre) o New Birth mezclaron psicodelia, melodía y funk sucio; Sylvia Robinson susurró «Pillow Talk» (1973) y Major Harris remató «Love Won’t Let Me Wait» con un orgasmo simulado.

scenes.name: Hip hop neoyorquino
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Con la música negra popular muerta estéticamente, el alma del pueblo pasó al underground: un funk ruidoso, áspero y tenso, demasiado desesperado para la radio negra. Los breaks de DJ Kool Herc en las fiestas de barrio del Bronx, Jazzy Jay, Afrika Bambaataa, DJ Hollywood, Grandmaster Flash y Eddie Cheeba convirtieron la mezcla de discos en arte: los chavales dejaron las bandas por dos platos, el scratch y los breaks repetidos, un collage posmoderno de toda la música grabada sobre un ritmo funky. Sylvia Robinson grabó en 1979 «Rapper’s Delight» de la Sugarhill Gang y fichó a Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five, cuya «The Message» (1982), con Melle Mel, dio voz a los sin voz como no se oía desde «What’s Going On»; siguieron «White Lines» o «New York, New York». Las cajas de ritmos dieron un funk industrial y minimalista (el bombo 808, «Five Minutes of Funk» de Whodini), y Run-D.M.C. («It’s Like That», «Rock Box», «King of Rock», «Walk This Way» con Aerosmith en Raising Hell, 1986) asaltó la radio rock, seguidos por los Beastie Boys.

podcast.title: Taylor Hawkins' First Group
podcast.body: Sylvia was Taylor Hawkins' very first musical group, based in Orange County, California. This band was formed in an area where reggae music was popular, and hard rock was generally "frowned upon." "His first group was in Orange County, if it called Sylvia."

xref.title: "The Eggman" Nickname Origin
xref.body: Eric Burdon, the leader of The Animals, acquired the nickname "the Eggman" after he disclosed details of an unusual oral sex act involving raw eggs, which he learned from his Jamaican girlfriend, Sylvia. This anecdote later found its way into The Beatles' song "I Am the Walrus," with John Lennon adopting the moniker. "And when he told everybody about it, he was immediately nicknamed the Eggman."

xref.title: Credit for Oasis's "Step Out"
xref.body: Following a court case over the similarities between his 1966 hit "Uptight Everything's All Right" and Oasis's "Step Out," Stevie Wonder, along with Sylvia Moe and Henry Cosby, received co-writing credits for "Step Out" and was awarded at least a quarter of the proceeds from any version of the song by Oasis. "Stevie Wonder gets a credit."

xref.title: Intellectual and Literary Figure
xref.body: Richie was the intellectual force behind the Manic Street Preachers, well-versed in figures like Karl Marx, Albert Camus, Sylvia Plath, Dostoevsky, JD Salinger, Jack Kerouac, and Joseph Conrad, as well as the Beat Poets. He meticulously rehearsed philosophical and literary quotes for interviews, solidifying his role as the band's literary expert. "Richie knew about Karl Marx, Albert Kamu, Sylvia Plath, Dostoevsky, JD Salinger, Jack Kerawak, Joseph Conrad, and all the beat poets."

xref.title: Step Out Lawsuit (Stevie Wonder)
xref.body: The song "Step Out" from "(What's the Story) Morning Glory?" resulted in a court case due to its resemblance to Stevie Wonder's 1966 hit "Uptight Everything's All Right." As a result, subsequent versions of "Step Out" include writing credits for Stevie Wonder, Sylvia Moe, and Henry Cosby, each entitled to at least a quarter of the proceeds. "Oasis was taken to court. And if you look at any post Morning Glory version of Step Out, like an Alive album or something, you'll see that it is listed as being written by No of Yalger and three other people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Studio Ownership and Academia
xref.body: Sylvia Massy owned her own studio for many years, which was a popular choice for bands like Sublime and Econoline Crush. Additionally, she has served as a visiting professor at Berklee College of Music and conducted workshops for the Abbey Road Institute, demonstrating her commitment to educating the next generation of audio professionals. "Sylvia owned her own studio for years, a place booked by Sublime, Econoline Crush and Dozens of Others."
